summaries.example: Imagine a group of people who are all human. “Human” is a common nature shared by them. Penbygull says this common nature is really present in the people, not floating somewhere by itself. A person can also be white, but “white” belongs directly to that individual. It can be connected to the shared human nature only indirectly, through the people who have it.
summaries.summary: William Penbygull was a late-medieval philosopher who worked in Oxford and defended many ideas associated with John Wyclif. His main topic was the relationship between universals and individuals. A universal is a shared nature, such as humanity; an individual is one particular thing, such as one person. Penbygull held that a universal exists in actual individuals and has no separate existence apart from them. He also said that a universal and its individuals are really the same in one respect, but different when considered as a shared kind and as particular things. To explain statements about these things, he developed a careful account of predication, or saying something of something else. He recognized direct statements, indirect statements based on shared parts, and causal statements. His theory of identity allowed things to differ while still sharing some of their underlying features.
key_ideas: Penbygull was a medieval thinker connected with the Oxford Realists and strongly influenced by John Wyclif.
He studied how shared kinds, such as humanity, relate to particular things, such as one person.
He said universals and individuals are really the same in one way but different in how we think about them.
He divided predication into formal, essential, and causal kinds.
His new account of identity helped explain how a shared nature and an individual could be related without being exactly alike in every respect.
summaries.why_it_matters: Penbygull shows how philosophers can use very careful definitions to solve a puzzle. If many people share humanity, does that make humanity one thing or many things? His answer tried to respect both sides: shared natures are real, but they do not exist separately from individuals. His ideas also show that a sentence can connect two things in different ways, not only by saying they are exactly the same.

important_terms.definition: A feature or nature that can be shared by many individual things, such as being human.
One particular thing, such as one person, rather than a shared kind.
Saying something about a subject, such as saying that Socrates is white.
A way two things can share some parts or features while still differing in others.

questions_to_think_about: Can two things be alike in some ways but different in others?
Is the word “human” only a name, or does it point to something real shared by people?
Why might it matter whether a quality belongs directly or indirectly to something?

summaries.example: Consider “Socrates is white” and “man is an animal.” In the first statement, whiteness is an accidental form: it belongs to an individual but is not part of what makes that individual human. Penbygull treats this as formal accidental predication when whiteness is directly present in Socrates. Yet he can also say that universal-man is white if at least one existing man is white. In that case, whiteness is attributed to the universal indirectly, through its individuals. The two statements therefore do not assert the same kind of relation.
summaries.summary: William Penbygull was an Oxford Realist whose surviving writings largely defend and refine John Wyclif’s philosophical program. The central problem is how universals can be real without becoming numerically separate objects, and how statements about them can avoid contradiction. Penbygull identifies three broad kinds of universals: metaphysical causes, concepts in the mind, and common natures existing in individuals. His real universals are actual features of individuals, but they have no being apart from those individuals. A universal and an individual are therefore really the same when viewed as a nature, while remaining formally distinct: the universal has generality, whereas the individual has thisness. This account requires a revised theory of predication. Formal predication involves direct presence of a form. Predication by essence involves partial identity and permits indirect attribution, such as calling universal-man white when at least one of its men is white. Causal predication concerns effects and their causes. Penbygull’s distinctive theory of identity distinguishes non-identity from difference and allows things that differ to share forms. Identity thus has a partial or graded dimension, rather than being only complete sameness.
key_ideas: Penbygull’s account begins from Wyclif and Robert Alyngton but modifies their treatment of predication.
He distinguishes metaphysical causes, mental universals, and real universals, with real universals existing in individuals outside the mind.
A real universal and its individuals are really identical as a nature, yet formally distinct because generality and thisness are opposed principles.
Formal predication requires direct presence of the relevant form; predication by essence expresses partial identity and can attribute an accidental form indirectly.
Causal predication concerns a relation in which the subject is caused by what the predicate signifies rather than containing that form.
Penbygull separates non-identity from difference and permits difference and real identity to be compatible, yielding degrees of distinction.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry illustrates a major medieval dispute about realism and nominalism: whether general natures exist in reality or are only names or concepts. Penbygull’s solution is not a simple choice between “exactly the same” and “entirely different.” By revising identity and predication together, he tries to explain how universals and individuals can overlap in metaphysical composition while supporting different kinds of statements. This is important for understanding how theories of language can depend on theories of what exists.

important_terms.definition: A common nature present in individual things and naturally suited to be predicated of more than one of them.
A particular entity, characterized by its “thisness,” or what makes it this individual rather than another.
The relation involved in saying a predicate of a subject; Penbygull analyzes it through metaphysical forms and identity.
Predication in which the form signified by the predicate is directly present in the subject.
Predication grounded in shared metaphysical components, even when the predicate is not directly present in the subject.
Predication in which the predicate is not present in the subject but the subject has been caused by what the predicate signifies.
A relation in which things share some constituent forms while differing in others.
The feature of a universal that makes it apt to be common, contrasted with an individual’s “thisness.”

questions_to_think_about: Does sharing many metaphysical constituents make two things partly identical, or merely similar?
Why does Penbygull need an indirect form of predication for claims about a universal and an individual’s accident?
How does his distinction between generality and thisness challenge an ordinary, all-or-nothing idea of identity?
What changes when predication is understood as a relation between metaphysical objects rather than simply membership in a set?

summaries.example: Suppose a class has several students, and some students are wearing white shirts. “Student” describes a kind shared by many people, while “Maya” names one individual. Penbygull would say the shared nature is real in the individuals, but it is not a separate object sitting somewhere apart from them. “Maya is wearing white” directly connects whiteness with Maya. Saying that the shared kind is white is different: it is true only indirectly, because at least one individual belonging to that kind is white.
summaries.summary: William Penbygull was a philosopher at Oxford around the end of the fourteenth and beginning of the fifteenth century. His writings mainly explain and defend the views of John Wyclif, but he also made an original contribution through a new theory of identity. Penbygull discusses universals, which are shared kinds or natures, and individuals, which are particular things. He accepts real universals: common natures exist in the individuals that have them, outside the mind, but not as separate beings. A universal and its individuals are really identical in one respect because they share a nature. They are formally distinct because a universal has generality while an individual has thisness. This creates a problem for predication. Not everything true of an individual can be said directly of its universal. Penbygull therefore distinguishes formal predication, predication by essence, and causal predication. His theory of identity explains how things may differ while sharing some of the same metaphysical forms.
key_ideas: Penbygull belonged to the Oxford Realist tradition and was a strong defender of Wyclif’s main philosophical ideas.
He recognized mental universals, real common natures in things, and higher metaphysical causes.
Real universals exist in actual individuals, not only as possibilities in the mind, but they do not exist separately from those individuals.
Universals and individuals are really the same as a nature while formally different as universal and individual.
Penbygull revised the kinds of predication so that direct, indirect, and causal connections could be distinguished.
His theory of identity allows difference without requiring complete separation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Penbygull helps us see why the question “Are general ideas real?” is more complicated than it first appears. His position tries to preserve the reality of shared natures without treating them as separate objects. It also connects metaphysics—the study of what exists—with logic—the study of how statements work. His account shows that deciding whether two things are identical may depend on which features are being compared.

important_terms.definition: A shared nature or kind that can be found in more than one individual.
A single, particular thing, such as one person or one object.
The philosophical act of saying that a predicate belongs to a subject.
The feature that makes a universal capable of being shared by many individuals.
The feature that makes an individual this particular thing and not another.
A relation in which two things share some underlying components but not all of them.

questions_to_think_about: If a common nature exists only in individuals, in what sense is it one universal?
Why might a philosopher distinguish being directly white from being white indirectly?
Can two things be partly the same and still be different things?
How could a theory of identity affect the meaning of an ordinary sentence?
